name: Adonijah
title: David's ambitious son and claimant to the throne
summary: As the fourth of David's sons, born to Haggith in Hebron, Adonijah emerged as the leading claimant to the throne after his older brothers Amnon and Absalom had died. In King David's final days, he took the initiative and declared himself the new king of Israel, supported by the commander Joab and the priest Abiathar. His attempt was nevertheless thwarted through the intervention of the prophet Nathan and Bathsheba, who reminded David of the promise that Solomon would inherit the throne. The event highlights an important theological principle in Israel's monarchy: succession to the throne was not determined by birthright, but by divine choice conveyed through the king's own word. After Solomon ascended the throne, Adonijah once again tried to strengthen his position by requesting Abishag of Shunem as his wife—a request that Solomon interpreted as a hidden claim to royal power. This final political misstep cost him his life, and Benaiah was sent to carry out the death sentence.

keyEvents.title: Adonijah Proclaims Himself King
keyEvents.description: After Absalom's death, Adonijah was the oldest surviving son of David and began to act as a claimant to the throne. He acquired chariots, horsemen, and fifty men who ran ahead of him, and secured support from the commander Joab and the priest Abiathar.

keyEvents.title: The Sacrificial Feast at En-Rogel
keyEvents.description: Adonijah arranged a great sacrificial feast at the Stone of Zoheleth near En-Rogel, where he invited his brothers and royal officials. Solomon, the prophet Nathan, Benaiah, and David's bodyguards were deliberately excluded from the invitation.

keyEvents.title: Nathan and Bathsheba Intervene with David
keyEvents.description: The prophet Nathan warned Bathsheba about Adonijah's plans, and together they went to the aging King David to remind him of his promise that Solomon would inherit the throne and sit on his royal seat.

keyEvents.title: Solomon Anointed as King
keyEvents.description: David ordered that Solomon be anointed king at the Gihon Spring by the priest Zadok and the prophet Nathan. The people's shouts of joy and the blast of trumpets reached Adonijah and his guests at En-Rogel, and the feast was dissolved in fear.

keyEvents.title: Adonijah Seeks Refuge at the Altar
keyEvents.description: When Adonijah learned that Solomon had been anointed king, he feared for his life and grabbed the horns of the altar. Solomon let him go with the promise that he would be spared as long as he proved himself worthy.

keyEvents.title: Adonijah's Request for Abishag and His Execution
keyEvents.description: After David's death, Adonijah approached Bathsheba with a request to have Abishag the Shunammite as his wife. When Bathsheba brought the matter before Solomon, the king interpreted this as a veiled attempt to claim the throne and ordered Benaiah to execute Adonijah.

versions.summary: Adonijah was the fourth son of King David, born to his wife Haggith. He attempted to make himself king over Israel in his father's final days but was passed over in favor of Solomon. His later attempt to secure power by requesting Abishag as a wife led to his execution on Solomon's orders.
versions.title: David's ambitious son
versions.reason: [major] Adonijah is himself listed as his own sibling. He should be removed from the siblings list.; [major] The role 'leader' is not precise enough for Adonijah. He was primarily a prince and claimant to the throne. The roles should be updated to better reflect this.; [minor] The life period of approximately 1010–970 BC is reasonable but somewhat uncertain. Adonijah was likely born around 1000 BC (David became king in Hebron around 1010, and Adonijah was his fourth son) and executed early in Solomon's reign (around 970–960 BC). An adjustment to approximately 1005–969 BC may be more accurate.; [minor] David had many sons. The list mentions only a few. In addition to Amnon, Absalom, Solomon, and Chileab, it is known from 2 Sam 3:2-5 and 1 Chr 3:1-4 that David also had sons such as Shephatiah and Ithream born in Hebron. These could usefully be included.; [major] The profile lacks footnotes. Interesting historical, linguistic, and theological notes about Adonijah should be added.; [minor] The summary is good but could be expanded somewhat to include the theological and political context surrounding the succession to the throne in Israel—that there was no automatic right of firstborn to the throne, but rather that the king himself appointed his successor.

versions.summary: Adonijah was the fourth son of King David, born to his wife Haggith. After the deaths of Amnon and Absalom, he was the eldest surviving heir to the throne and attempted to make himself king over Israel in his father's final days. Despite support from the army commander Joab and the priest Abiathar, he was passed over in favor of Solomon, whom David himself had appointed as his successor. Adonijah's story illustrates that succession to the throne in Israel did not automatically follow the right of the firstborn, but depended on the king's – and in a deeper sense God's – choice. His later attempt to secure influence by asking for Abishag of Shunem as his wife was interpreted as a political power grab and led to his execution at Solomon's command.
versions.title: David's ambitious son and claimant to the throne
versions.reason: [minor] The summary is good but structurally very similar to version 1 with the same opening ('Adonijah was David's fourth son, born of his wife Haggith'). It should be rephrased to clearly distinguish it from the earlier version.; [minor] Event 2 ('Adonijah holds a sacrifice feast at En-Rogel') overlaps significantly with event 1, since verses 9–10 are included in both. Consider merging them or clarifying the distinction between the two events.; [minor] The list of siblings is limited to David's sons mentioned in 2 Sam 3:2–5 plus Solomon. David had many more sons (cf. 1 Chr 3:1–9), including those born in Jerusalem such as Nathan, Sheba, and others. The list is not incorrect but could note that this is a selection of half-siblings.; [minor] Footnote 3 refers to Exod 21:13–14, but the most direct reference to the altar's horns as a place of refuge is found in Exod 21:14. Verse 13 deals with places of refuge in general, not specifically the altar. The reference is acceptable but could be clarified.; [minor] A lifespan of approximately 1005–969 BC gives an age of about 36 years. This is reasonable, though the dating is uncertain. Adonijah was born after Amnon, Chileab, and Absalom in Hebron (2 Sam 3:4), that is, early in David's reign. The birth date seems a bit late if David began to reign in Hebron around 1010 BC. A slightly earlier birth date (for example, around 1008) might be more precise, but this falls within reasonable uncertainty.

footnotes.text: The name Adonijah (Hebrew: אֲדֹנִיָּה, Adoniyyah) means 'my lord is YHWH' or 'Yahweh is my lord.' This theophoric name reflects a declaration of piety, which is ironic given Adonijah's self-exalting ambitions.

Adonijah's attempt to obtain Abishag the Shunammite as his wife (1 Kings 2:13-25) was interpreted by Solomon as a political claim to the throne. In the ancient Near East, it was customary for a new king to take over his predecessor's harem as a sign of transfer of power. Similarly, Absalom had demonstrated his assumption of power by going in to David's concubines (2 Sam 16:21-22).

Adonijah's grasping the horns of the altar (1 Kings 1:50) was a known practice in ancient Israel for seeking asylum. The altar served as a place of refuge, and holding onto the altar's horns signaled that one sought divine protection. This practice is also regulated in the legislation of Exodus, where the altar is mentioned as a place where a murderer shall not have the right to asylum in cases of intentional killing (Exod 21:14).

En-Rogel, the place where Adonijah held his sacrificial feast, was a spring southeast of Jerusalem at the confluence of the Hinnom and Kidron valleys. The site is identified with Bi'r Ayyub (Job's Well) and had strategic and religious significance in ancient Jerusalem.

In ancient Israel, succession to the throne did not automatically follow the right of the firstborn. The king had the right to appoint his successor, which often led to conflicts. David's choice of Solomon, his younger son by Bathsheba, over older sons like Adonijah is an example of this and reflects a theological theme of God's sovereign election that runs throughout Scripture.

The text in 1 Kings 1:6 notes that David had never rebuked Adonijah. The Hebrew expression used here (לֹא־עֲצָבוֹ אָבִיו) suggests that David had never caused him pain or discomfort through correction. This pattern of lack of discipline is repeated in David's family and provides a psychological background for Adonijah's rebellious actions.

The Gihon spring, where Solomon was anointed as a counterweight to Adonijah's ceremony at En-Rogel, was Jerusalem's most important water source. Archaeological excavations have uncovered an extensive water system connected to this spring, including what is traditionally identified as Warren's Shaft. The choice of this location for Solomon's anointing was strategic—it lay closer to the City of David and had strong symbolic ties to the city and royal power.
